headline: Funding flows. Bureaucracy expands. Satellites stall.
deck: This week highlights funding successes alongside bureaucratic inertia in space.

stories.head: True Anomaly raises $190M amid defense demand
stories.body: True Anomaly has secured a $190 million Series C funding round, bringing its valuation to $1.6 billion as demand for co-orbital security and space domain awareness continues to grow. The company is well-positioned to capitalize on increasing DoD interest in its capabilities, which may soon become a staple in government contracts. In a sector where cash flow often trumps innovation, this funding illustrates the defense establishment's appetite for security solutions.
stories.soWhat: Investors are clearly betting that the future of space security is lucrative, even if the tech itself remains a work in progress.

stories.head: Air Force tackles troubled GPS receiver program
stories.body: The Air Force has taken control of a GPS receiver program that has faced significant challenges, including delays and technical difficulties. This intervention suggests a renewed commitment to rectifying past failures, but it also raises questions about how much longer the military will tolerate setbacks in critical navigation systems. With the stakes high, the agency's ability to turn this program around will be closely monitored.
stories.soWhat: If the Air Force can't fix this GPS mess, we might as well start handing out compasses.

stories.head: Office of Space Commerce advances mission authorization
stories.body: The Commerce Department is moving forward with a voluntary mission authorization system aimed at unregulated space activities, highlighting the federal government’s ongoing struggle to keep pace with the rapid evolution of the space sector. While this initiative may streamline some processes, it also underscores the tendency of bureaucracy to expand in parallel with innovation. The implications for startups operating in the gray areas of space law could be significant.
stories.soWhat: Bureaucracy in space is like gravity—it's always there, and it can slow down even the fastest rockets.

watchlist.title: Keep an eye on Sierra Space's timeline
watchlist.body: With the Dream Chaser DoD variant passing its design review, the real test will be whether they can stick to a credible flight schedule.

watchlist.title: Monitor Copernicus imagery release delays
watchlist.body: The EU's hold on Copernicus data could impact various stakeholders relying on timely satellite imagery, especially in defense and environmental sectors.

watchlist.title: Anduril and L3Harris partnership developments
watchlist.body: Their bid for the tactical SDA constellation could reshape the competitive landscape, making it essential to track their progress.

watchlist.title: Watch for GPS jamming trends
watchlist.body: With GPS jamming in the Eastern Med returning to pre-2024 levels, this could signal shifts in operational tactics for both military and commercial entities.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
